vulnerabilities.title: FORMAT_STRING

root_cause.description: In vuln_func, user input read via scanf("%s", buf) into a stack buffer at rbp-0x70 is passed directly as the format string argument to printf (printf(buf)) at address 0x12c9. The first argument register rdi is loaded with the address of buf (lea rax,[rbp-0x70]; mov rdi,rax) and printf is called with no separate format string constant. This means attacker-controlled input is interpreted as the printf format string, enabling format specifiers like %p (arbitrary stack read), %s (arbitrary string read via pointer), and %n (arbitrary memory write). S1 confirmed at runtime that user input appears at the 7th format argument position (offset 6), meaning attacker-controlled data on the stack is directly accessible as printf arguments.

affected_objects: stack return address (writable via %n if address known)

attack_surface.input: stdin via scanf("%s", buf) at rbp-0x70
data_flow: stdin -> scanf("%s", buf) writes attacker input to stack buffer at rbp-0x70
buf (rbp-0x70) loaded into rdi as first argument to printf at 0x12c1-0x12c9
printf interprets buf as format string, processing %p/%s/%n specifiers
User input bytes appear at 7th format argument position (offset 6) on stack
Attacker can embed target addresses in format string payload at offset 6 and use %n to write to those addresses, or %p/%s to read

security_check.expected: printf should be called with a constant format string (e.g., printf("%s", buf)) so user input is treated as data, not as format specifiers.
security_check.actual: printf is called with buf as the format string argument (printf(buf)), no format string constant is used. No validation of input for format specifiers is performed.
security_check.missing_or_incorrect: Missing format string constant. The code should use printf("%s", buf) or equivalent, but instead passes user input directly as the format string.

vulnerable_operation.expression: printf(buf) where buf = [rbp-0x70] = attacker input from scanf("%s")
vulnerable_operation.target: Stack memory (via %p read), arbitrary memory at attacker-specified addresses (via %s read / %n write), BSS variables including can_leave at 0x401c (via %n write)
vulnerable_operation.size: unlimited (format string processed until null terminator in buf)

impact.reason: Format specifier %p in the user-controlled format string causes printf to output stack values, including the stack canary (at rbp-0x8, reachable via %p at the appropriate offset), saved return addresses (containing PIE base offset), and saved rbp values. This leaks sensitive information that can be used to bypass ASLR/PIE and stack canary protections. S1 runtime confirmed %p leaks stack values.

Format specifier %n in the user-controlled format string causes printf to write the number of bytes printed so far to a memory address specified by a format argument. Since user input is at offset 6, an attacker can embed a target address in the format string payload and use %n to write to it. Writable targets include BSS variable can_leave (0x401c) and potentially the stack return address. Full RELRO prevents GOT writes, but BSS and stack remain writable.

Via %n write to can_leave (BSS 0x401c), an attacker could set this never-written variable to a nonzero value, changing program control flow to enable loop exit (see BUG-003). This corrupts the intended program logic state.

evidence.description: Disassembly at 0x12bd: lea rax,[rbp-0x70]; 0x12c1: mov rdi,rax; 0x12c4: mov eax,0x0; 0x12c9: call printf@plt. The buffer buf at rbp-0x70 (containing user input from scanf) is loaded directly into rdi (first argument) and passed to printf with no format string constant. This is a direct format string vulnerability.

Disassembly at 0x12a0: lea rax,[rbp-0x70]; 0x12a4: mov rsi,rax; 0x12a7: lea rax,[rip+0xda8] (points to "%s"); 0x12ae: mov rdi,rax; 0x12b6: call scanf@plt. scanf reads unbounded input into buf at rbp-0x70, which is then used as printf's format string. The input source is confirmed as attacker-controlled stdin.

S1 runtime confirmed that %p format specifiers in user input cause stack value leaks, and user input bytes appear at the 7th format argument position (offset 6): 0x70252e70252e7025 = first bytes of '%p.%p.%p'. This confirms the format string is processed with user-controlled specifiers and user data is accessible as format arguments.

Full RELRO (confirmed via checksec and .got section analysis) means GOT entries at 0x3f80-0x4000 are read-only at runtime, preventing GOT overwrite via %n. However, BSS section (0x4010-0x4020) including can_leave at 0x401c remains writable (RW-), making it a viable %n write target. Stack memory is also writable.

verification_required: Verify that glibc 2.39 on this system permits %n format specifier (some builds disable it via FORTIFY or tunables; FORTIFY not detected in binary but runtime behavior needs S3 dynamic confirmation)
Determine exact stack layout at format argument offsets 1-6 to identify which sensitive values (canary, return address, PIE base pointer) are leakable via %p
Verify that can_leave at BSS 0x401c can be written to a nonzero value via %n, and that this enables loop exit

vulnerabilities.title: STACK_BUFFER_OVERFLOW

root_cause.description: In vuln_func, scanf("%s", buf) is called twice (at 0x12b6 and 0x12f3) to read user input into a stack buffer at rbp-0x70. The %s format specifier reads input until whitespace with no length limit. The buffer is 0x68 (104) bytes before the stack canary at rbp-0x8. An input longer than 104 bytes will overflow past the buffer into the canary, saved rbp, and return address. The stack canary provides detection, but the format string vulnerability (BUG-001) can leak the canary value via %p before the overflow, potentially allowing the attacker to overwrite the canary with its correct value and continue overwriting the return address.

vulnerable_operation.operation: scanf("%s") unbounded write to stack buffer

impact.reason: Input exceeding 104 bytes overwrites the stack canary at rbp-0x8. If the canary value is known (leakable via format string %p from BUG-001), the attacker can overwrite it with the correct value, then overwrite saved rbp and return address, causing memory corruption of the stack frame.
If the canary is overwritten with an incorrect value, __stack_chk_fail is called at 0x132c, terminating the process. This is a denial of service via crash.

evidence.description: Disassembly: 0x12a0: lea rax,[rbp-0x70]; 0x12a4: mov rsi,rax; 0x12a7: lea rax,[rip+0xda8] (points to "%s" at 0x2056); 0x12b6: call scanf@plt. The format string is "%s" with no field width, reading unbounded input into buf at rbp-0x70.

Stack frame setup: 0x127e: sub rsp,0x70 allocates 0x70=112 bytes. 0x1282: mov rax,fs:0x28; 0x128b: mov [rbp-0x8],rax places canary at rbp-0x8. Buffer at rbp-0x70 is 0x68=104 bytes before canary. Overflow of >104 bytes reaches canary.

Canary check: 0x131d: mov rax,[rbp-0x8]; 0x1321: sub rax,fs:0x28; 0x132a: je 0x1331 (ok); 0x132c: call __stack_chk_fail. If canary is corrupted, __stack_chk_fail is called. The canary value at rbp-0x8 is within the format string %p leak range (BUG-001), enabling potential canary bypass.

CET shadow stack (SHSTK) is enabled (confirmed via checksec). Shadow stack provides hardware protection of return addresses independent of the stack canary. Even if the canary is bypassed via format string leak and the return address on the stack is overwritten, the shadow stack may detect the mismatch on ret. This constrains but does not eliminate the impact of stack buffer overflow. The overflow still causes memory corruption of the stack frame regardless.

vulnerabilities.title: UNREACHABLE_EXIT_CONDITION

root_cause.description: The vuln_func loop exit condition at 0x1309-0x131a requires BOTH strcmp(buf, "--")==0 AND can_leave!=0. The global variable can_leave (BSS 0x401c, 4-byte int) is initialized to 0 and is only READ at address 0x1312 (mov eax, [can_leave]) — it is never WRITTEN by any instruction in the entire binary. Since can_leave is always 0, the condition 'can_leave != 0' (test eax,eax; je 0x12bd) always jumps back to the loop body. The loop can never exit via the normal code path. The program runs indefinitely until alarm(60) kills it with SIGALRM. This is a logic error: the exit gate variable is never set, making the intended exit path unreachable.

root_cause.description: The function get_shell at address 0x125c calls system("/bin/sh") but has no callers in the binary's control flow graph. It is dead code — never invoked through any normal execution path. Its presence as an unreachable function that directly spawns a shell makes it a target for control flow hijacking: if an attacker can redirect control flow to get_shell (e.g., via format string %n overwrite of a return address or function pointer, or via stack buffer overflow return address overwrite), it provides immediate shell execution. get_shell begins with endbr64 (0x125c), making it a valid indirect branch target under CET/IBT.

attack_surface.input: Control flow redirection via format string %n (BUG-001) or stack buffer overflow (BUG-002)
attack_surface.entry_function: get_shell (not called normally; potential hijack target)
data_flow: get_shell at 0x125c is dead code with no callers in CFG
get_shell calls system("/bin/sh") at 0x126e
If control flow is redirected to get_shell via format string %n write to return address or via stack overflow, system("/bin/sh") executes
get_shell starts with endbr64, satisfying CET/IBT indirect branch target requirements
PIE base must be leaked first (via format string %p) to compute absolute address of get_shell

security_check.expected: Functions that execute shell commands should not exist in a production binary unless properly guarded by authentication/authorization.
security_check.actual: get_shell exists as dead code with no callers and no access control. It calls system("/bin/sh") unconditionally.
security_check.missing_or_incorrect: Presence of unguarded shell-spawning function. While not directly callable, it serves as a ready-made target for control flow hijacking.

impact.reason: get_shell itself is not a vulnerability — it is dead code. Its impact is only realized if combined with a control flow hijacking vulnerability (BUG-001 format string %n or BUG-002 stack overflow). If control flow is redirected to get_shell, system("/bin/sh") executes. This is a theoretical impact dependent on successful exploitation of BUG-001 or BUG-002. S2 does not assess exploit feasibility — this is recorded as a contributing factor for downstream analysis.

evidence.description: Disassembly: 0x125c: endbr64; 0x1260: push rbp; 0x1261: mov rbp,rsp; 0x1264: lea rax,[rip+0xd9d] (points to "/bin/sh" at 0x2008); 0x126b: mov rdi,rax; 0x126e: call system@plt; 0x1273: nop; 0x1274: pop rbp; 0x1275: ret. Function calls system("/bin/sh") unconditionally.

S1 CFG analysis confirms get_shell has no callers — it is not called from main, vuln_func, init, or any other function. It is dead code. The function begins with endbr64 (0x125c), satisfying CET/IBT indirect branch landing pad requirements, making it a valid target for indirect branch redirection if control flow hijacking is achieved.

verification_required: This is not independently exploitable — it requires a control flow hijacking vulnerability (BUG-001 or BUG-002) to redirect execution to get_shell
PIE base must be leaked to compute the absolute address of get_shell (0x125c + PIE base)
CET shadow stack (SHSTK) may prevent return address overwrite from redirecting to get_shell; this needs S3/S4 assessment

non_vulnerabilities.description: init() calls setvbuf(stdout, 0, _IONBF, 0) to disable stdout buffering and alarm(60) for timeout. No user input is processed. No memory safety issues.
non_vulnerabilities.reason: No attacker-controlled input reaches this function. setvbuf and alarm are called with constant arguments. No vulnerability.

non_vulnerabilities.description: main() calls init() then vuln_func(), returns 0. No direct input processing or memory operations.
non_vulnerabilities.reason: main only dispatches to init and vuln_func. No vulnerability in main itself; all attack surface is in vuln_func.

non_vulnerabilities.description: strcmp(buf, "--") at 0x1309 compares user input against the literal string "--". strcmp is used correctly with proper null-terminated strings. The comparison is full (not strncmp/prefix), and the return value is correctly checked (test eax,eax; jne).
non_vulnerabilities.reason: strcmp is called with correct arguments and its return value is properly handled. No partial match, truncation, or return value misuse. The strcmp check itself is not a vulnerability — the logic error is in the can_leave condition (BUG-003), not in strcmp.

unresolved.description: Whether format string %n write is functional in this glibc 2.39 runtime environment
unresolved.reason: Some glibc versions/builds disable %n via _FORTIFY_SOURCE or GLIBC_TUNABLES. FORTIFY is not detected in the binary (checksec confirms fortify=false), but glibc 2.39 may have runtime %n restrictions that cannot be determined from static analysis alone.
unresolved.required_next_step: S3 dynamic verification: test %n format specifier behavior at runtime by sending a %n payload and observing whether a write occurs.

unresolved.description: Exact semantic identity of stack values at format string argument offsets 1-6
unresolved.reason: S1 runtime confirmed user input at offset 6 (7th argument), but the identity of values at offsets 1-5 (whether they include canary, return address, saved rbp, libc pointers) requires dynamic analysis with known PIE base to interpret.
unresolved.required_next_step: S3 dynamic analysis: leak stack values via %p at each offset, correlate with known PIE/libc base to identify canary, return address, and other sensitive pointers.

unresolved.description: Whether CET shadow stack (SHSTK) effectively prevents return address control via stack overflow or format string %n
unresolved.reason: SHSTK is enabled (confirmed via checksec). Shadow stack provides hardware-level return address protection that operates independently of the stack canary. Even if the canary is bypassed and the stack return address is overwritten, the shadow stack may detect the mismatch on ret and terminate the process. This constrains control flow hijacking but does not prevent memory corruption or information leakage.
unresolved.required_next_step: S3/S4 assessment of CET shadow stack impact on exploit feasibility. S2 notes this as a mitigation constraint on BUG-002 and BUG-004 impact.

unresolved.description: Whether external seccomp sandbox or other runtime restrictions are active
unresolved.reason: No seccomp-related symbols or prctl calls found in the binary. An external sandbox may be imposed by the execution environment but cannot be verified from binary analysis alone.
unresolved.required_next_step: S3 runtime environment assessment for seccomp/sandbox presence.
